chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
title: Convincing Paul Jeffries that Eric Dolphy matched Charlie Parker
summary: Dolphy had a big sound and developed themes; a student set Dolphy against Parker.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: But aren't there exceptions? I mean, there must be some kids out there who want to -- let's say, some bass players who play Charles Mingus records.
Well, wh a about this kid I heard on tenor?
We have no ________ foundation. I like to hear his writing, because what he was doing was symphonic solos. Long lines, all by himself, and no background. He (inaudible) about Charlie Parker dying.
Paul is teaching background, which he teaches Charlie Parker. He has two --(unintelligible).
He had a student come up and say he thought that -- Sue, grab that caviar.
This kid said that he thought Charlie Parker -- every ________ contributed more to jazz than Charlie Parker.
Where would Eric have been without
So Paul spent a whole lot of time trying to show the kid Eric Dolphy was nowhere near Charlie Parker.
And so I put out some records that Paul never heard of Eric Dolphy.

And I changed his mind about Eric Dolphy. I said, first of all, Eric Dolphy is the only alto player I know who had a big sound like Charlie Parker. Charlie Parker and Ben Webster (unintelligible). You hear him in person?
So did Eric Dolphy. Eric played so loud they had to put him behind the curtain one time on a tune.
I remember on that date we did, the engineer was going crazy because of Eric.
And Paul had never heard good Eric Dolphy. And Eric -- he kept asking me, he said, you don't
think Eric is as good as Bird? Well, I really do, man.
I think he contributed as much. I know he came through Bird and tried to play Bird and he never played Bird as good as McPherson did.

But he got something out of Bird. Paul was laughing because Eric kept playing all the things he could already play, in a repetitive riff. (Singing.) Then he'd go and come back -- (singing). Every time he played that phrase, I said, Paul, (unintelligible).

That's when you take a theme and develop it. He's not trying to play like Charlie Parker, a different note, a different __________ every time. I brought his respect up for Eric Doffey more, I know I did.
Yeah. It's funny that even Paul wouldn't have known.
